passage: The cooperative bank in Tasgaon pulled its shutters down for lunch at one, but Ayesha stayed at her desk with the crop-loan files. By three the ceiling fan was pushing hot air around, and head office had sent back six forms for a missing stamp. Ayesha typed fast: "If your team read the forms properly, we wouldn't waste days." Her finger hovered over send. Everything felt pointless; maybe she wasn't cut out for this job at all. Chandrika leaned over the partition with a steel box. "You haven't eaten. Methi thepla. Eat, then send." Ayesha almost refused, then ate two. Ten minutes later she read the email again and winced. She deleted it and wrote, "Six forms need stamps; we'll send them by Thursday." The job looked like a job again, not a disaster.

qa.q: How many forms did head office send back?
qa.a: Six forms, for a missing stamp.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling as her finger hovered over send?
qa.a: She felt irritated and hopeless, as if she wasn't cut out for the job, after working through lunch.

qa.q: What made the difference before the email went out?
qa.a: Eating Chandrika's thepla and rereading the email ten minutes later, which let her see how harsh it was and write a calm one instead.

qa.q: How might the head office team have felt if the first email had gone?
qa.a: They would likely have felt insulted and defensive, turning a small stamp problem into a bigger conflict.

grounding: Shows a professional who skips lunch to finish work nearly sending a harsh email and feeling hopeless, until food shrinks the problem back to size.

passage: Freya had promised herself a proper lunch, but the client in Kraków wanted the whole brochure redone by six, so she ate nothing but half an apple at her desk. By four the screen seemed to swim. When Olga messaged, "Small change: can the logo be bigger?", Freya's chest went tight. She typed, "Maybe you'd like to design it yourself?" and deleted it, then sat staring, sure the project and possibly her career were a disaster. On the way to the printer she passed the office kitchen, saw the bread and soup left from the team lunch, and remembered she was running on half an apple. She ate a bowl standing up. Back at her desk, the logo change took four minutes. She replied, "Done. Anything else before six?"

qa.q: What had Freya eaten by four?
qa.a: Nothing but half an apple.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when Olga asked for a bigger logo?
qa.a: Her chest went tight with irritation, and she felt hopeless, sure the project and maybe her career were a disaster.

qa.q: What could Freya try the next time a deadline eats her lunch?
qa.a: Stop to eat before answering requests, because a change that felt huge on an empty stomach took only four minutes after the soup.

qa.q: How would Olga have felt if the sharp reply had been sent?
qa.a: Olga would probably have felt hurt and confused, since the request was small and politely worded.

grounding: Shows a professional working through lunch, nearly sending a harsh reply and feeling hopeless, until food makes the problem look its real size.

passage: At the community centre in Jaipur, the eye-camp registrations had doubled, and Tarun had worked straight through lunch at the front desk. By four his head throbbed. When the volunteer group chat asked who was bringing the extra chairs, he typed, "Do I have to do everything myself? Nobody here takes anything seriously," and hit send. Then he sat with his face in his hands, sure the whole camp would collapse. Himani, the coordinator, put a plate of poha and a glass of chaas in front of him. "Eat. Then we look at it." Twenty minutes later the camp looked manageable; two volunteers had already offered chairs. Tarun opened the chat again. "Sorry for that message, everyone. I'd skipped lunch and got nasty. Thank you for the chairs."

qa.q: What did Himani put in front of Tarun?
qa.a: A plate of poha and a glass of chaas.

qa.q: How was Tarun feeling with his face in his hands?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and overwhelmed, sure the whole camp would collapse, after working through lunch.

qa.q: Was Tarun right to apologise even after he had eaten, and why?
qa.a: Yes; hunger explained the harsh message but did not excuse it, so owning it repaired trust with the volunteers.

qa.q: How might the volunteers have felt reading the first message?
qa.a: They were likely stung and unfairly blamed, since two of them were already offering chairs.

grounding: Shows a worker who skips lunch sending a harsh message and feeling hopeless, then seeing the problem shrink once he has eaten.

passage: Camila got home at eight to find Dalia at the table, laptop full of flats in Montevideo. "So, I've found three. Can we decide tonight?" Camila heard her own voice come out flat and sharp: "Tonight? Seriously?" She stopped, one hand still on her bag. She hadn't eaten since a coffee at eleven. "Sorry. That came out mean. I'm starving, and I don't trust myself with a big decision right now. Can I eat first, and we look properly at nine?" Dalia closed the laptop halfway. "Okay. There are leftover empanadas." At nine, with food inside her, Camila felt curious instead of cornered. She liked the second flat. And before they started, she said, "Sorry again about the tone earlier. Hungry isn't an excuse."

qa.q: What was on Dalia's laptop?
qa.a: Flats in Montevideo.

qa.q: What did Camila feel when she heard herself say "Tonight? Seriously?"
qa.a: She noticed a sharp, irritable edge in her voice and felt wary of trusting herself with a big decision while starving.

qa.q: Why is Camila's second apology at nine important?
qa.a: It shows that eating first protects the conversation but does not excuse the rude tone; she still owns it.

qa.q: How might Dalia have felt when Camila asked to wait until nine?
qa.a: Dalia may have been a little disappointed but reassured, since Camila explained why and promised a proper look soon.

grounding: Shows a person hearing the edge in her own voice, eating before a big decision, and still apologising for the rudeness afterwards.

passage: The feedback meeting with Sudha was set for 12:30 in the small glass room at the call centre, and Sonali walked in with the error report and an empty stomach. Sudha had barely sat down when Sonali heard herself say, "Do you even read the scripts?" Sudha's face went still. Sonali turned the report face-down. "That was unfair, and I'm sorry. I've had no breakfast and I'm cranky, and you deserve a clearer head than this. Can we meet at two instead?" Sudha nodded, relieved but wary. At two, after rice and dal in the canteen, Sonali began again: "Sorry about earlier. Let's go through the three errors together and see what's confusing in the script." They found that one line in the script was actually wrong.

qa.q: Where was the feedback meeting set?
qa.a: In the small glass room at the call centre, at 12:30.

qa.q: What made Sonali stop and turn the report face-down?
qa.a: She heard the edge in her own voice, felt ashamed of being unfair, and recognised that hunger was making her cranky.

qa.q: Why did moving the meeting help both of them?
qa.a: Sonali could give feedback with a steady head, and together they found the real cause, a wrong line in the script, instead of fighting.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when the meeting restarts at two?
qa.a: Sudha is likely relieved and less defensive, since Sonali apologised again and invited her to work through the errors together.

grounding: Shows a manager noticing the edge in her voice, postponing a hard conversation until she has eaten, and still apologising for the rudeness.

passage:
Dear Mahima,
I owe you a proper reply about Ammi and Abbu's anniversary dinner, and an apology for Sunday's call.
When you asked about the guest list, I snapped that you always make things complicated. That wasn't fair. I'd been on the road since six without eating, and I heard the edge in my voice even as I said it. That's why I ended the call so suddenly: I went to eat before I said something worse.
Now, fed and calmer, here's what I actually think. Your idea of a small dinner at home is better than the hall. Ammi hates crowds. I'd only add Chacha's family.
From now on, if I sound like that, tell me to eat and call you back. I'll do the same for you.
Your brother,
Wasim

qa.q: What does Wasim think of Mahima's idea?
qa.a: That a small dinner at home is better than the hall.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel on hearing the edge in his own voice?
qa.a: Wasim felt uneasy and sorry, aware of being hungry and afraid of saying something worse, so he ended the call to eat.

qa.q: What makes Wasim's plan for the future helpful?
qa.a: Agreeing that either can say "eat and call back" lets them pause hungry conversations, while Wasim's apology shows it does not excuse rudeness.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt after the call ended so suddenly?
qa.a: Mahima may have felt hurt and confused by the snap and the abrupt ending, until reading this explanation.

grounding: Shows Wasim noticing the edge in a hungry voice, eating before continuing a hard conversation, and apologising for the rudeness afterwards.

passage: The Saturday market in Seville was baking hot, and Fatima had been choosing tomatoes for an hour. Lucia, in the pushchair, had stopped singing. She whined, pushed away her toy rabbit, then drooped against the strap, eyes heavy. "Tired already?" Fatima frowned, then saw Lucia's dry lips. The water bottle was still full in the basket. She held it to Lucia's mouth. Lucia gulped and gulped. A few minutes later she was pointing at the oranges again.

qa.q: Where was the water bottle?
qa.a: Still full in the basket.

qa.q: How was Lucia feeling before she drank?
qa.a: She was fussy and drowsy, uncomfortable in the heat but unable to say she was thirsty.

qa.q: What small habit could Fatima use on hot market days?
qa.a: Offer water regularly, not only when Lucia seems upset, because a toddler cannot ask.

qa.q: How might Fatima have felt seeing the full bottle?
qa.a: Probably a pang of guilt, then relief as Lucia gulped and perked up.

grounding: Shows a thirsty toddler turning fussy and drowsy on a hot day, and a drink of water rescuing her mood.

passage:
Monday: May heat in Delhi. By afternoon Lalit clung to Vishal's leg, whining, too sleepy to play but too fussy to nap.
Wednesday: The same again. Then Vishal noticed the sippy cup, still half full from the morning. He offered it. Lalit drank it all and said, "More!"
Friday: Vishal filled the cup at every meal and in between. Lalit spent the afternoon pushing his toy truck round the room, humming.

qa.q: What was still half full from the morning?
qa.a: The sippy cup.

qa.q: What does Lalit's clinging and whining on Monday suggest?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable and fussy, likely thirsty in the heat but unable to explain it.

qa.q: What rhythm helped on Friday?

qa.q: What might Monday afternoon be like for Vishal?

grounding: Shows a toddler in hot weather becoming fussy, sleepy and clingy from thirst, and regular water offered through the day fixing it.

passage: The pandal crowd in Kolkata pressed hot and loud around them, and Thomas, two, had turned into a limp, grumpy bundle on Bidisha's hip. He cried when she tried to put him down and cried when she held him. She felt his forehead, then checked his nappy. Nothing. Then she remembered: no drink since the auto ride. She bought a small bottle of water at a stall and held it to his lips. He drank in long, noisy gulps, then patted her cheek and pointed at the drums.

qa.q: When had Thomas last had a drink?
qa.a: Not since the auto ride.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he cried whether held or put down?
qa.a: He was fussy and uncomfortable, thirsty in the hot crowd but unable to say what was wrong.

qa.q: What can busy parents take from Bidisha's afternoon?
qa.a: Offer water regularly on hot, crowded days, since a toddler cannot ask and thirst can look like tiredness.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel after checking and finding nothing wrong?
qa.a: Puzzled and a little worried, until she remembered the missing drink.

grounding: Shows a thirsty toddler on a hot, busy day turning fussy and clingy, and a drink of water rescuing him.

passage: Liam spent every minute of lunch chasing the ball across the dusty oval in Adelaide, shirt stuck to his back. He didn't stop at the drinking fountain; the game was too close. In maths his head began to throb. He snapped at Ines when she borrowed his ruler, then put his head down on his arms. "Did you drink anything at lunch?" Ines whispered. He thought. Nothing since breakfast. Mrs Park let him go to the fountain, and he drank for a long time. By the end of the lesson the throbbing had faded. That night he put his blue bottle next to his school shoes, and the next day he clipped it to the fence by the pitch.

qa.q: Where did Liam clip his bottle the next day?
qa.a: To the fence by the pitch.

qa.q: What was Liam feeling in maths?
qa.a: He felt headachy, tired and grumpy, enough to snap at Ines, without knowing thirst was the cause.

qa.q: What habit did Liam start, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Putting his bottle by his shoes and clipping it by the pitch, so he notices thirst and drinks even when the game is exciting.

qa.q: How might Ines have felt when Liam snapped about the ruler?
qa.a: Ines may have felt stung, but instead of snapping back she asked a caring question that helped.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild playing hard in the sun, forgetting to drink, feeling headachy and grumpy, and learning to carry a bottle.

passage: Parade practice for Republic Day ran all morning on the school ground, and Vishal marched in the front row, proud of his white shoes. His water bottle stayed in his bag in the classroom. By eleven his forehead ached and his legs felt heavy. He stamped the wrong foot twice, then muttered, "This is stupid," when Rekha Ma'am corrected him. She looked at his flushed face. "When did you last drink water?" He couldn't remember. She sent him to the shade with her own bottle and called a water break for the whole group. That afternoon Vishal wrote WATER on the back of his hand in pen. The next day his bottle came out to the ground with him.

qa.q: What did Vishal write on the back of his hand?
qa.a: WATER.

qa.q: Why did Vishal mutter "This is stupid"?
qa.a: He felt headachy, heavy and grumpy after marching in the sun without drinking, so a correction felt irritating.

qa.q: What did Rekha Ma'am do that helped more than scolding?
qa.a: She noticed his flushed face, asked about water, and gave the whole group a water break.

qa.q: How might Rekha Ma'am see Vishal's muttering?
qa.a: She reads it as a sign of thirst and heat rather than rudeness.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild exercising in the sun without drinking becoming achy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry a bottle.

passage:
Monday: Anand played gully cricket in the afternoon sun for three hours and came home with a headache, snapping at his brother Varun over the TV remote.
Wednesday: Same game, same headache. Mamma asked what he had drunk. "Nothing, I wasn't thirsty." But his lips were cracked, and he drained two glasses at once.
Saturday: Anand took a bottle to the lane and drank at every change of innings. Varun, keeping score, reminded him too. That evening he had no headache, and he let Varun choose the channel.

qa.q: When did Anand drink on Saturday?
qa.a: At every change of innings.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling on Monday evening?

grounding: Shows a child playing in the sun without drinking getting headachy and grumpy, then learning to notice thirst and carry water.

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage: Dhruv was usually the loudest voice on the basketball court behind the colony school in Chennai, first to every loose ball. Today, forty minutes into drills under a white-hot sky, Coach Harish watched him jog instead of sprint, miss easy layups, and snap "I know!" when a teammate called the play. Harish felt the old urge to blow the whistle and give a speech about attitude. Instead he looked at the sideline. Dhruv's bottle stood there, still sealed. "Water break, everyone. Five minutes, in the shade." He tossed Dhruv the bottle. "All of it." Dhruv drank, sat against the wall, and after five minutes grinned for the first time that afternoon. That night Harish added a water whistle every fifteen minutes to the practice plan.

qa.q: What did Harish notice about Dhruv's bottle?
qa.a: It was still sealed.

qa.q: What was Harish tempted to do, and why did he change his mind?

qa.q: What is practice like for Dhruv before the break?

grounding: Shows a coach seeing a keen teen turn slow and sharp after training in heat without water, and choosing a water break over a pep talk.

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage:
Coach Chetan blew his whistle. "Neelam! That's the third pass you've dropped."
"I'm trying, Sir!"
"You're dragging your feet. Where's the fire from last week?"
"I don't know. My head hurts and everyone's annoying me."
"Everyone?"
"Everyone. Priya won't stop talking."
"Hm. When did you last drink water?"
"At lunch? Maybe."
"It's four o'clock and baking out here. Sit in the shade. Drink half this bottle, slowly."
"I'm fine."
"You're thirsty. Drink."
Five minutes later:
"Sir, my head's better. Sorry for snapping."
"Not your fault. New rule, whole team: water break every fifteen minutes."

qa.a: Four o'clock.

qa.q: What made Chetan suspect thirst rather than laziness?

subtype: Sports practice fatigue and short temper [Observer]
passage: I've coached under-16 football in Margao for six years, and I still think about one afternoon with Naveen. He was my most excited player, the kind who arrives early and begs for extra shooting practice. That day, in the April heat, he trailed behind in every drill, kicked a cone away when I corrected him, and told a younger boy to stop following him around. I nearly benched him for attitude. Then I saw him leaning on the goalpost, eyes half shut, lips dry. He had forgotten his bottle and was too proud to ask to borrow one. I sat him in the shade with water and a wet towel and called a break for everyone. Twenty minutes later he was laughing again. I'm Farida, and my first question to a grumpy player now is, "Have you had water?"

qa.q: What had Naveen forgotten?
qa.a: His bottle.

qa.q: How did Farida feel before spotting the dry lips, and what changed?
qa.a: Farida felt annoyed enough to bench him for attitude, then grew concerned on seeing him leaning on the goalpost with his eyes half shut and lips dry.

qa.q: What does Farida's first question to a grumpy player show?
qa.a: That checking for water and rest comes before blaming attitude, because a body need often explains the mood.

qa.q: Why might Naveen not have asked to borrow a bottle?
qa.a: He was too proud to ask, perhaps embarrassed to admit he had forgotten it.

grounding: Shows a coach noticing an eager teen become slow and sharp in the heat without water, and rest and water changing the mood more than a lecture.

Wednesday: Same slump, same chai. Leela pushed her own steel bottle across the table. "When did you last drink water?" Seema honestly couldn't remember. She drank half the bottle, walked once round the quad, and came back able to read a whole page.
Friday: Seema brought her own bottle and set an hourly reminder on her phone. At three, instead of the canteen, she refilled it at the cooler. The afternoon fog never came.

subtype: Mistaking thirst for tiredness or hunger [Actor]
passage: Ira, you keep yawning over that laptop and reaching for another biscuit. Let me tell you something. When I was twenty, I worked the afternoon shift at the Coimbatore mill. Hot as an oven. Every day around three my eyes went heavy and my hands went slow on the loom, and I'd run to the tea stall. Two cups, sugar, a bun. And I'd feel worse. One day old Muthu, the foreman, found me half asleep at the loom. He didn't shout. He handed me his clay pot of water and said, "Drink this first. Tea later." I drank it all and stood outside in the breeze for five minutes. My head cleared like a window wiped clean. After that I kept a pot of water under my loom, and your Shankar Thatha was the only one on the shift who didn't nod off. So, drink some water first, and then see if you're really hungry.

qa.a: The afternoon shift at the Coimbatore mill.

qa.q: What was young Shankar feeling around three each day?
qa.a: He felt heavy-eyed and sluggish, and mistook it for tiredness or hunger, reaching for tea and a bun.

qa.q: What turning point changed Shankar's afternoons at the mill?
qa.a: When Muthu handed him water instead of shouting and he drank it and stood in the breeze, the fog lifted, so Shankar began keeping water under his loom.

qa.q: How did Muthu see the young man half asleep at the loom?
qa.a: Muthu saw a thirsty worker rather than a lazy one, which is why he offered water instead of shouting.

grounding: Shows a young worker mistaking thirst for tiredness or hunger, reaching for tea and snacks, until water and a short break clear the fog.

subtype: Mistaking thirst for tiredness or hunger [Actor]
passage: The power had been off in the girls' hostel since noon, the water cooler was dead, and the exam was tomorrow. Ritu sat on the floor with her notes, working through a packet of chips and two cups of canteen coffee, still feeling as if her brain were wrapped in cotton. "I think I need more food," she told Sarika, reaching for the biscuits. Sarika looked at the empty bottle by Ritu's knee. "You haven't had water since breakfast. The cooler's off, remember?" Ritu blinked. They walked down to the shop by the gate in the heat and bought two big bottles. Ritu drank slowly on the steps, then sat in the breezy corridor for ten minutes. When she opened her notes again, the words stayed still. She put the biscuits away.

passage: Rekha, that's your fourth cup of tea since lunch and not one glass of water. I know, because I used to be you. When I joined this firm thirty years ago, I lived on office chai: a kettle in the morning, a flask in the afternoon. By six I'd have a thumping headache, snap at the office boy for a slow file, and go home sure this job was killing me. I even started looking at other companies. Then our old accountant, Mrs D'Souza, began putting a steel jug of water on my desk every morning without a word. For a week I ignored it. The next week I drank it, just to be polite. The headaches faded. I stopped snapping. And I stayed. Pradeep Sir, thirty years and one steel jug. So, here's a glass. Humour an old man.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Souza put on Pradeep's desk?
qa.a: A steel jug of water, every morning.

qa.a: Young Pradeep felt irritable and worn down, with a thumping headache, and was convinced the job was killing him.

qa.a: When he finally drank the water Mrs D'Souza left, his headaches faded and he stopped snapping, so he stayed instead of blaming the job.

qa.q: How might Mrs D'Souza have seen young Pradeep?
qa.a: She seemed to notice young Pradeep was running on chai alone, and cared enough to leave water quietly every morning.

grounding: Shows a desk worker living on tea, ending the day headachy and snappish and blaming the job, until regular water changes the mood.

passage: The water dispenser on the fourth floor had been broken since Monday, festive-season complaints were pouring in, and Shreya had survived the day on three machine coffees. By five her head was pounding, every customer sounded rude, and she typed a message to her sister: "I hate this job. Quitting after Diwali." She didn't send it; she just stared at it, feeling flat and grey. Then Asif came back from the shop downstairs with a crate of water bottles for the team. "Dispenser's still dead. Everyone drink one. Boss's orders." Shreya drank a whole bottle, then half of another, and stretched by the window. Twenty minutes later the headache had eased, and the next customer sounded merely confused, not rude. She deleted the message and put a bottle on her desk for tomorrow.

qa.a: Since Monday.

qa.a: She felt flat and grey, with a pounding head, and irritated enough to blame the job and think of quitting.

qa.q: How does Asif see the team's long day?
qa.a: Asif notices that nobody has had water with the dispenser dead, and quietly solves it for everyone.

grounding: Shows a desk worker drinking only coffee, ending the day headachy and flat and blaming the job, until water lifts the mood.

passage: Aditi's work-from-home days in their Andheri flat followed a pattern: a flask of masala chai at nine, another at two, back-to-back calls in between. By seven she would close the laptop with a headache, snap at Santosh for asking about dinner, and say, "This job is draining me." One evening Santosh put a big glass bottle of water on her desk before her first call. "Just an experiment. Finish this by lunch, and another by five." She rolled her eyes but sipped it between calls. By Friday she noticed something odd: no seven o'clock headache, and she had laughed at Santosh's terrible joke about the neighbour's parrot. "It's just water," she said, surprised. "It's just water," Santosh agreed, grinning.

qa.q: When did Aditi drink masala chai?
qa.a: At nine and at two.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she noticed the change on Friday?
qa.a: She felt surprised and lighter, laughing at Santosh's joke without the usual headache.

qa.a: It set a simple target for water during the day, which eased the headaches and short temper she had blamed on the job.

qa.q: What were those evenings like for Santosh before the experiment?
qa.a: He was snapped at over a simple dinner question and probably felt pushed away and worried about her.

grounding: Shows a professional drinking only tea through long workdays, blaming the job for headaches and low patience, and being surprised by the payoff of regular water.

passage:
Thursday, 10 pm
Something's off, and I've stopped pretending it isn't. For about a month I've been exhausted even after long nights of sleep. And thirsty, weirdly thirsty, finishing a whole bottle and still wanting more. I've tried everything I can think of: early nights, less screen, more water, fewer coffees. Nothing has changed.
Tonight Lalit found me asleep on the sofa at eight with my shoes on. He said, very gently, "Arohi, this isn't a willpower thing. Please get it checked." I wanted to argue that I'm just busy. But I've been saying that for a month.

passage: Imran taught Class 8 maths at the zilla parishad school in Wai, and for six weeks he had dragged himself through each day. He slept early. He drank from the matka in the staffroom so often the other teachers joked about it. Still he felt heavy, and still his mouth felt dry. He told himself it was the heat, then the new syllabus, then his age, though he was only twenty-five. One Sunday his friend Yogesh watched him doze off mid-sentence over tea at the stall. "Enough guessing, Imran. You rested, you drank. It's not working. We're going to the doctor at the district hospital tomorrow. I'll come on the bus with you." Imran opened his mouth to argue, then closed it. On Monday he took half a day's leave, and they caught the eight o'clock bus to Satara together.
